orig_9709_m1_forces_force_models.description: Isolate a particle, identify external forces, use model assumptions and apply Newton’s third law.

sections.title: How do I decide which arrows belong in a force diagram?
sections.label: Isolate one body
sections.intro: Choose the body first. For each arrow, name the external agent that exerts the force and its effect on the chosen body. A particle diagram uses a single point for the body.

blocks.html: A taut string pulls along the string, away from the particle. A rigid strut in compression pushes along the strut. Weight acts vertically downwards, while contact can exert a normal reaction and friction.

figure.alt: A central particle has upward tension T and downward weight W.
figure.caption: Only the string and Earth exert forces on the hanging particle. Their arrows are \(T\) and \(W\).

blocks.html:
Model wordConsequence
ParticleDraw forces through one representative point. Rotation is outside the model.
Light stringThe string's own weight is negligible. When taut, it exerts a pull at its attachment.
Inextensible stringIts length does not change. This says nothing about the magnitude of its tension.
Smooth contactThere is no tangential friction component.
Do not put both bodies' forces on one particle diagram. Forces exerted by the chosen particle on its surroundings belong elsewhere.

blocks.title: Select the forces on one body
blocks.prompt: Isolate the calibration block. It rests on a smooth level platform. A vertical string is taut and pulls it upwards while it remains in contact. Which list gives the forces acting on it?

options.second: Weight, tension, normal reaction and friction.

blocks.hint: The block still touches the platform, so include its normal force. A smooth platform supplies no friction.
blocks.solution:
The block still touches the platform, so include its normal force. A smooth platform supplies no friction.

The force list is: weight, tension and normal reaction.

sections.title: Why must weight be stated in newtons?
sections.label: Convert mass to weight
sections.intro: Mass measures how much matter is in the particle. Weight is the gravitational force on it. The equation \(W=mg\) converts a mass and local gravitational acceleration into a force.

blocks.html: Use kilograms for \(m\), metres per second squared for \(g\), and newtons for \(W\). Use the value of \(g\) stated in the question.
An arrow labelled just with the mass in kilograms is missing the factor \(g\).

blocks.title: Convert mass to weight
blocks.prompt: Find the weight of a \(\frac{12}{5}\,\mathrm{kg}\) recording unit. Take \(g=10\) metres per second squared.
blocks.hint: Multiply the value in kilograms by g to give the force in newtons.
blocks.solution:
Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.

Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{12}{5}\times10=24\).

The weight is \(24\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

sections.title: What changes when contact is smooth?
sections.label: Read the contact model
sections.intro: A smooth surface supplies no tangential force. It can still prevent penetration by exerting a normal reaction. A rough contact may also exert a force parallel to the surface.

blocks.html: In a force diagram, draw the normal reaction at a right angle to the contact surface. It points vertically upwards on a horizontal table, but away from an inclined surface at an angle to the vertical. A rough surface can have zero friction if no tangential resistance is needed.
Do not invent a friction arrow simply because a floor is rough. Inspect the other forces first.

blocks.title: Read the smooth-contact assumption
blocks.prompt: A test weight rests on a smooth horizontal table. Which statement describes the force the table exerts on the weight?

options.normal: It acts vertically upwards, perpendicular to the table.
options.vertical: It acts horizontally along the table.

blocks.hint: Draw the table first. Its tangent is horizontal, so its normal is vertical.
blocks.solution: A smooth table has no friction. While the weight presses on the table, the reaction acts away from it, vertically upwards.

sections.title: How do I find an equal and opposite partner?
sections.label: Use Newton's third law
sections.intro: Each interaction involves two bodies. The force one exerts on the other has an equal and opposite partner of the same kind. The pair appears on two different free-body diagrams.

blocks.html: If \(A\) pushes \(B\) with a particular force, \(B\) pushes \(A\) with the same magnitude and an opposite direction.

figure.alt: Force arrows at bodies A and B point in opposite horizontal directions.
figure.caption: Each arrow acts on a different body. These are two separate force diagrams showing the two sides of the same contact interaction.

blocks.html: Weight and normal reaction may be equal in a particular equilibrium, but both act on the same body and have different agents.
Write ‘force of A on B’. Interchange A and B to name its partner.

blocks.title: Find the partner of weight
blocks.prompt: A tool case rests on a bench. What is the Newton's third-law partner of its weight?

options.earth: The pull of the tool case on the Earth.
options.bench: The upwards force of the bench on the tool case.
options.push: The downwards force of the tool case on the bench.

retry.feedback: The bench acts on the same object as weight. The partner of weight acts on the Earth.

blocks.hint: Weight is the Earth's gravitational pull on the tool case.
blocks.solution:
Weight is the Earth's gravitational pull on the tool case.

The partner is the gravitational pull of the tool case on the Earth, with equal magnitude and opposite direction. The bench's normal force is a separate contact interaction.

sections.title: What does equilibrium say about vertical or horizontal forces?
sections.label: Balance one axis
sections.intro: In equilibrium the resultant force is zero. With forces along one axis, choose a positive direction, then add the signed forces. A body at rest or moving with constant velocity can be in equilibrium.

blocks.html: On one axis write \(\sum F=0\), with opposite senses given opposite signs.
Zero velocity at an instant is insufficient evidence of equilibrium. The body must remain at rest or move with constant velocity.

blocks.title: Balance a vertical force equation
blocks.prompt: A instrument of weight \(64\,\mathrm N\) is in equilibrium on a horizontal tray. The upward normal force is \(42\,\mathrm N\), and a vertical string is taut. Find the tension in the string.
blocks.hint: The upward forces add to the weight. They do not each equal the weight.
blocks.solution:
Draw only the forces on the instrument: weight downwards, tension and normal reaction upwards.

Resolve upwards. \(R+T-W=0\), so \(R+T=64\).

The tension is \(22\,\mathrm N\).

glossary.definition: A model treating the body’s forces as acting at a single point.
The part of a contact force perpendicular to the surface.
A pull along a taut string or cable.
The local gravitational force on the body.

examples.title: Select the forces on one body
examples.question: Isolate the beacon. It is suspended at rest from a vertical string. There is no other contact. Which list gives the forces acting on it?
solution: The Earth and the taut string are the only agents exerting forces on the beacon.
The force list is: weight and upward tension.

examples.title: Convert mass to weight
examples.question: Find the weight of a \(\frac{7}{4}\,\mathrm{kg}\) measuring unit. Take \(g=10\) metres per second squared.
solution: Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.
Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{7}{4}\times10=\frac{35}{2}\).
The weight is \(\frac{35}{2}\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

examples.title: Convert mass to weight
examples.question: Find the weight of a \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{kg}\) sample carrier. Take \(g=\frac{49}{5}\) metres per second squared.
solution: Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.
Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{3}{2}\times\frac{49}{5}=\frac{147}{10}\).
The weight is \(\frac{147}{10}\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

examples.title: Read the smooth-contact assumption
examples.question: A display panel is in contact with a smooth incline. What does the model imply about the contact force?
solution: A smooth contact has no friction component parallel to the surface.
The normal reaction is still present when the surface is pressing on the body. It points perpendicular to the surface.

examples.title: Select the forces on one body
examples.question: Isolate the moving trolley. It is guided along a smooth horizontal track. A taut horizontal string pulls forward. Neglect air resistance. Which list gives the forces acting on it?
solution: The guide can press normally while its smooth contact supplies no tangential force.
The force list is: weight, normal reaction and tension.

examples.title: Identify the third-law partner
examples.question: A guide rail exerts a contact force of \(21\,\mathrm N\) to the left on a wheeled frame. Which force is its Newton's third-law partner?
solution: A third-law pair comes from the same interaction. Interchange the body exerting the force and the body receiving it.
Preserve the magnitude and reverse the direction. a wheeled frame exerts \(21\,\mathrm N\) to the right on A guide rail.

examples.title: Balance a vertical force equation
examples.question: A tool holder of weight \(42\,\mathrm N\) rests on a horizontal platform while a vertical string pulls it upwards with tension \(16\,\mathrm N\). Find the normal force exerted by the platform.
solution: Draw only the forces on the tool holder: weight downwards, tension and normal reaction upwards.
Resolve upwards. \(R+T-W=0\), so \(R+T=42\).
The platform exerts \(26\,\mathrm N\) upwards.

revision.body:
Choose the method

UseWhat to write
Weight\(W=mg\), vertically down and measured in newtons.
Normal reactionAway from the surface, perpendicular to it.
Smooth contactThere is no friction component along the surface.
Third-law pairEqual magnitude, opposite direction, same interaction and different receiving bodies.
One-axis equilibriumGive the two senses opposite signs and write \(\sum F=0\).
revision.checks:
• Name who exerts each force.
  • Convert kilograms to newtons before balancing forces.
  • Keep third-law partners on separate diagrams.
revision.examTip: If two forces balance on one body they need not form a third-law pair. To find a partner, swap the agent and receiver.

extraPractice.title: Interpret equilibrium from motion
extraPractice.prompt: A barge travels along a straight channel at constant speed. What can you conclude about the resultant force on the small barge?
extraPractice.hint: It moves with constant velocity because its speed and direction both remain unchanged.
extraPractice.solution:
It moves with constant velocity because its speed and direction both remain unchanged.

Its forces are in equilibrium, just as for a body that stays at rest.

extraPractice.title: Convert mass to weight
extraPractice.prompt: Find the weight of a \(\frac{8}{5}\,\mathrm{kg}\) steel insert. Take \(g=10\) metres per second squared.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the value in kilograms by g to give the force in newtons.
extraPractice.solution:
Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.

Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{8}{5}\times10=16\).

The weight is \(16\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

extraPractice.title: Read the smooth-contact assumption
extraPractice.prompt: A slider presses against a smooth inclined plane. Which statement describes the force the plane exerts on the slider?

options.normal: It acts perpendicular to the surface.
options.vertical: It acts vertically upwards, regardless of the slope.

extraPractice.hint: Draw a line along the incline. The normal is at a right angle to that line.
extraPractice.solution: A smooth incline exerts its reaction away from the surface, at a right angle to the slope. The incline is not level, so the reaction is not vertical.

extraPractice.title: Identify the third-law partner
extraPractice.prompt: A loading arm exerts a contact force of \(36\,\mathrm N\) upwards on a support pad. Which force is its Newton's third-law partner?

options.partner: a support pad exerts \(36\,\mathrm N\) downwards on A loading arm.
options.same_body: A loading arm exerts \(36\,\mathrm N\) downwards on a support pad.
options.same_direction: a support pad exerts \(36\,\mathrm N\) upwards on A loading arm.

extraPractice.hint: A third-law pair comes from the same interaction. Interchange the body exerting the force and the body receiving it.
extraPractice.solution:
A third-law pair comes from the same interaction. Interchange the body exerting the force and the body receiving it.

Preserve the magnitude and reverse the direction. a support pad exerts \(36\,\mathrm N\) downwards on A loading arm.

extraPractice.title: Find a missing horizontal force
extraPractice.prompt: A crate is at rest. It has a pull of \(45\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and two leftwards forces, one of \(16\,\mathrm N\) and one unknown. Find the unknown magnitude.
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the two leftwards forces from the rightwards force and set the signed total equal to zero.
extraPractice.solution:
At equilibrium the horizontal component total is zero.

Take rightwards as positive: \(45-16-X=0\).

The remaining leftwards force is \(29\,\mathrm N\).

orig_9709_m1_forces_resolving_forces.description: Resolve signed components, combine forces and calculate the direction of a resultant or balancing force.

sections.title: Which component uses cosine?
sections.label: Resolve from the given axis
sections.intro: Draw the angle between the force arrow and the reference direction. The adjacent component has magnitude \(P\cos\theta\), while the opposite component has magnitude \(P\sin\theta\). Apply directional signs afterwards.

blocks.html: The reference determines the trig function. Cosine accompanies the stated reference axis, whether it is horizontal, vertical or tilted.

figure.alt: An angled force P points up and right. A right triangle shows the horizontal projection P x and vertical projection P y.
figure.caption: The labelled angle \(\theta\) is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal component is \(P\cos\theta\).

blocks.html: Do not automatically use cosine for horizontal. Check which line the angle is measured from.

blocks.title: Resolve an angled force
blocks.prompt: A force of \(26\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) towards the right of the upward vertical. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{5}{12}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.

retry.feedback: This uses cosine for the horizontal component. The reference for this angle is vertical.

blocks.hint: Look at the stated reference axis before choosing sine and cosine. Use negative signs for leftwards or downwards.
blocks.solution:
The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.

\(\cos\theta=\frac{12}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{5}{13}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.

The rightwards component is \(10\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(24\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(26\sin\theta\) and \(26\cos\theta\).

sections.title: How do I handle downward or leftward components?
sections.label: Use signed components
sections.intro: Choose positive directions before resolving. An angle used in a right triangle gives positive side lengths, so those lengths need signs to show direction.

blocks.html: A negative component means it points against the corresponding positive axis. The magnitude of the full force remains non-negative.
Adding positive side lengths without checking directions can change both the resultant size and its direction.

blocks.title: Resolve an angled force
blocks.prompt: A force of \(39\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) below the horizontal to the right. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{12}{5}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.

retry.feedback: The force points downwards, so its upwards component is negative.

blocks.hint: Look at the stated reference axis before choosing sine and cosine. Use negative signs for leftwards or downwards.
blocks.solution:
The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.

\(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{12}{13}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.

The rightwards component is \(15\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(-36\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(39\cos\theta\) and \(-39\sin\theta\).

sections.title: How do I combine forces pointing in different directions?
sections.label: Add along each axis
sections.intro: Resolve each force along the same pair of perpendicular axes. Add rightwards components to obtain the horizontal total and upwards components to obtain the vertical total.

blocks.html: Find \(S_x\) and \(S_y\) first. The magnitude is \(\sqrt{S_x^2+S_y^2}\).
Adding magnitudes gives an incorrect resultant unless all force arrows point in the same direction.

blocks.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
blocks.prompt: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(-6\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(13\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(10\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-9\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Find the rightwards and upwards components of the resultant, and its exact magnitude.
blocks.hint: Add the signed components on each axis. Take the magnitude only after the component totals are found.
blocks.solution:
\(S_x=-6+\left(10\right)=4\) and \(S_y=13+\left(-9\right)=4\).

The magnitude follows from Pythagoras using the two resultant components.

The signed components are \(4\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(4\,\mathrm N\) upwards. The magnitude is \(4 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm N\).

sections.title: How do I state a resultant's direction?
sections.label: Name the angle reference
sections.intro: The component signs identify the quadrant. Use the right triangle of component magnitudes to calculate an acute reference angle, then identify which axis and side that angle describes.

blocks.html: When the horizontal component is non-zero, the reference angle to a horizontal ray has tangent \(\frac{|S_y|}{|S_x|}\). State above or below and right or left explicitly.
A number followed by a degree symbol is incomplete if the reference ray is not clear.
Keep unrounded components until the final angle. When required, give degrees to one decimal place.

blocks.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
blocks.prompt: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(14\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-5\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(-2\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-7\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Give the magnitude of the resultant exactly and its angle below the horizontal to the right, to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Add the signed components on each axis. Take the magnitude only after the component totals are found.
blocks.solution:
\(S_x=14+\left(-2\right)=12\) and \(S_y=-5+\left(-7\right)=-12\).

The magnitude is \(\sqrt{S_x^2+S_y^2}=12 \sqrt{2}\).

Use \(\tan\theta=1\). The resultant has magnitude \(12 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm N\) and acts at \(45.0^\circ\) below the horizontal to the right.

sections.title: What force would cancel the resultant?
sections.label: Find an equilibrant
sections.intro: An added force produces equilibrium when it cancels the existing resultant on both axes. It has the same magnitude as the resultant and points in the opposite direction.

blocks.html: The balancing components are \(-S_x\) and \(-S_y\). Test that adding the new force gives zero on each axis.
Reversing just one component generally reflects the arrow instead of reversing it.

blocks.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
blocks.prompt: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(-11\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(7\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(3\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-4\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Give the two signed components of the additional force that produces equilibrium.
blocks.hint: Add the signed components on each axis. Take the magnitude only after the component totals are found.
blocks.solution:
\(S_x=-11+\left(3\right)=-8\) and \(S_y=7+\left(-4\right)=3\).

An additional force must cancel each component of the resultant separately.

The additional force has rightwards component \(8\,\mathrm N\) and upwards component \(-3\,\mathrm N\).

glossary.definition: The signed part of a force along a chosen axis.
The single force equivalent to all the given forces combined.
An additional force equal and opposite to the existing resultant.

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(25\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal to the right. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
solution: The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.
\(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.
The rightwards component is \(20\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(15\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(25\cos\theta\) and \(25\sin\theta\).

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(50\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) below the horizontal to the left. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
solution: The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.
\(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.
The rightwards component is \(-40\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(-30\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(-50\cos\theta\) and \(-50\sin\theta\).

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(63\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) towards the left of the upward vertical. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{12}{5}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
solution: The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.
\(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{12}{13}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.
The rightwards component is \(- \frac{756}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(\frac{315}{13}\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(-63\sin\theta\) and \(63\cos\theta\).

examples.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
examples.question: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(14\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(5\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(-8\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(3\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Find the rightwards and upwards components of the resultant, and its exact magnitude.
solution: \(S_x=14+\left(-8\right)=6\) and \(S_y=5+\left(3\right)=8\).
The magnitude follows from Pythagoras using the two resultant components.
The signed components are \(6\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(8\,\mathrm N\) upwards. The magnitude is \(10\,\mathrm N\).

examples.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
examples.question: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(8\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(12\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(-14\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-4\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Find the rightwards and upwards components of the resultant, and its exact magnitude.
solution: The magnitude follows from Pythagoras using the two resultant components.
The signed components are \(-6\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(8\,\mathrm N\) upwards. The magnitude is \(10\,\mathrm N\).

examples.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
examples.question: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(6\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(10\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(11\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(2\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Give the magnitude of the resultant exactly and its angle above the horizontal to the right, to one decimal place.
solution: \(S_x=6+\left(11\right)=17\) and \(S_y=10+\left(2\right)=12\).
The magnitude is \(\sqrt{S_x^2+S_y^2}=\sqrt{433}\).
Use \(\tan\theta=\frac{12}{17}\). The resultant has magnitude \(\sqrt{433}\,\mathrm N\) and acts at \(35.2^\circ\) above the horizontal to the right.

examples.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
examples.question: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(15\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-8\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(-4\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(2\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Give the two signed components of the additional force that produces equilibrium.
solution: An additional force must cancel each component of the resultant separately.
The additional force has rightwards component \(-11\,\mathrm N\) and upwards component \(6\,\mathrm N\).

revision.body:
Choose the method

UseWhat to write
Adjacent to the angleUse \(P\cos\theta\) for the magnitude.
Opposite the angleUse \(P\sin\theta\) for the magnitude.
ResultantAdd signed components. Magnitude is \(\sqrt{S_x^2+S_y^2}\).
DirectionUse \(\tan\theta=\frac{|S_y|}{|S_x|}\) when \(S_x\ne0\). Interpret the quadrant.
EquilibriumThe additional balancing components are \(-S_x,-S_y\).
revision.checks:
• Read the angle reference before resolving.
  • Keep signs and exact values until the final calculation.
  • Name the ray and side when giving a direction.
revision.examTip: Start with a small sketch showing the reference angle and chosen positive axes.

sections.title: How do I resolve weight on an incline?
sections.label: Choose slope axes
sections.intro: Use one axis up the line of greatest slope and the other normal to the plane. Weight remains vertical in the diagram. The two component magnitudes come from the angle between vertical and the inward normal.

blocks.html: For inclination \(\alpha\), the weight component down the plane is \(W\sin\alpha\), and the component into the plane is \(W\cos\alpha\).
The incline is not inclined relative to the weight direction by \(\alpha\). Look for the angle between the weight and the inward normal.

blocks.title: Resolve weight on a slope
blocks.prompt: A particle has weight \(65\,\mathrm N\). A plane makes angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). Find the two magnitudes of the weight components downhill and into the plane.
blocks.hint: On a nearly level plane the downhill component is small. The expression using sine of the slope angle has that behaviour.
blocks.solution:
The weight points vertically downwards. Its angle to the inward normal is \(\alpha\).

sections.title: How does a string along the slope hold a particle?
sections.label: Balance along the plane
sections.intro: On a smooth plane the tension can balance the downhill component of weight. If the string is parallel to the plane it has no normal component and only weight presses into the plane.

blocks.html: Resolve uphill for \(T=W\sin\alpha\) and away from the plane for \(R=W\cos\alpha\) in this particular model.

figure.alt: Weight points down, normal reaction points out perpendicular to the slope, and string tension points up the slope.
figure.caption: Use axes along and perpendicular to the incline. Tension has no normal component in this arrangement.

blocks.html: These equations assume the string is parallel to the plane. A tilted string changes both balance equations.

blocks.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(52\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.
blocks.hint: Choose axes along and normal to the slope. Use both balance equations and check whether the tension changes the reaction.
blocks.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(20\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(48\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

Tension is along the plane, so it has no normal component.

Resolve uphill. \(T=20\) gives \(T=20\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(0\right)T=48\) gives \(R=48\).

The tension is \(20\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(48\,\mathrm N\).

sections.title: What changes when the string is horizontal?
sections.label: Resolve horizontal tension
sections.intro: The horizontal tension \(T\) makes angle \(\alpha\) with the slope. The component along the slope points uphill, and the perpendicular component presses the particle into the plane.

blocks.html: When the pull is horizontal, the equations are \(T\cos\alpha=W\sin\alpha\) and \(R=W\cos\alpha+T\sin\alpha\).

figure.alt: A particle is supported by a slope. Weight W points vertically down, reaction R points perpendicular to the slope, and tension T points horizontally right. Angle alpha is between T and the upslope direction. Dashed projections separate the uphill and inward components of T.
figure.caption: The dashed triangle resolves the horizontal tension into \(T\cos\alpha\) uphill and \(T\sin\alpha\) into the plane. The inward component adds to the normal load from the weight.

blocks.html: An uphill horizontal pull does not lift the particle away from an incline. Draw its normal component pointing inwards.

blocks.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(80\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls horizontally towards the higher side of the plane. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.

retry.feedback: This accounts only for weight. The horizontal tension also pushes into the incline.

blocks.hint: Choose axes along and normal to the slope. Use both balance equations and check whether the tension changes the reaction.
blocks.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(48\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(64\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

The horizontal tension resolves to \(T\cos\alpha\) uphill and \(T\sin\alpha\) into the incline.

Resolve uphill. \(\frac{4}{5}T=48\) gives \(T=60\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(- \frac{3}{5}\right)T=64\) gives \(R=100\).

The tension is \(60\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(100\,\mathrm N\).

sections.title: When can tension reduce the normal reaction?
sections.label: Resolve a tilted string
sections.intro: A string directed above the slope has an outward component. Use the angle between string and slope, which can differ from the angle of the slope itself.

blocks.html: If tension makes angle \(\beta\) above the slope, then \(T\cos\beta=W\sin\alpha\) and \(R+T\sin\beta=W\cos\alpha\).
A surface cannot pull the particle towards itself. If your normal reaction would be negative, the assumed contact model fails.

blocks.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(78\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls uphill at angle \(\beta\) above the line of greatest slope, measured in the vertical cross-section. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The acute angle \(\beta\) satisfies \(\tan \beta=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.

blocks.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(30\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(72\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

The tension resolves to \(T\cos\beta\) uphill and \(T\sin\beta\) away from the incline.

Resolve uphill. \(\frac{4}{5}T=30\) gives \(T=\frac{75}{2}\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)T=72\) gives \(R=\frac{99}{2}\).

sections.title: How do two tilted strings balance a hanging load?
sections.label: Resolve a junction
sections.intro: Take the junction as the particle. The strings pull up and away from it, and the vertical load pulls down. Angles can differ, so the tensions need not match.

blocks.html: The two horizontal components cancel. The two upward components add to the load.
A light junction contributes negligible weight of its own, but the stated load still acts on it.
Show a horizontal equation and a vertical equation before solving for the tensions.

blocks.title: Balance two strings at a junction
blocks.prompt: A light junction carries a vertical load of \(96\,\mathrm N\). One taut string slopes up to the left at \(\alpha\) above the horizontal, and a second slopes up to the right at \(\beta\). The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The acute angle \(\beta\) satisfies \(\tan \beta=\frac{4}{3}\). Find the tension in each string.
blocks.hint: The horizontal components oppose each other. The two upward components add to the weight.
blocks.solution:
The string tensions act away from the junction. The vertical load acts downwards.

Resolve horizontally: \(\frac{4}{5}T_L=\frac{3}{5}T_R\). Resolve vertically: \(\frac{3}{5}T_L+\frac{4}{5}T_R=96\).

Use the horizontal equation to write \(T_R=\frac{4}{3}T_L\). Substitute this into the vertical equation.

The left tension is \(\frac{288}{5}\,\mathrm N\) and the right tension is \(\frac{384}{5}\,\mathrm N\).

sections.title: How much friction does a particle at rest actually need?
sections.label: Calculate the required friction
sections.intro: First find the force that would unbalance the particle along the surface if friction were absent. Static friction supplies the opposite force if it lies within the available limit.

blocks.html: At rest, determine the friction from \(\sum F_{\parallel}=0\). Then test \(|f|\le\mu R\), where \(f\) denotes signed friction.
Using \(F=\mu R\) in every question can invent an unbalanced force on a particle already at rest.

blocks.title: Resolve before using the friction limit
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(60\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough horizontal floor. A force of \(8\,\mathrm N\) acts to the right, parallel to the floor. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the normal reaction, the friction magnitude required for equilibrium and the maximum friction. Decide whether the particle can be in equilibrium.

retry.feedback: That is the available limit. The friction needed for horizontal equilibrium balances the applied force.

blocks.hint: An applied force can change the normal reaction. Balance vertically before finding the friction limit.
blocks.solution:
Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Resolve the applied force: \(8\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(0\,\mathrm N\) upwards.

Vertical equilibrium gives \(R=60\). Then \(\mu R=20\).

The required friction is less than the maximum. The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

The normal reaction is \(60\,\mathrm N\), required friction is \(8\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(20\,\mathrm N\). The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

sections.title: How do I recognise limiting equilibrium?
sections.label: Identify the limit
sections.intro: A resting particle is in limiting equilibrium when the friction required just equals the maximum possible magnitude. Any extra demand in the same direction would break the balance.

blocks.html: ‘On the point of sliding’ or ‘about to slip’ indicates \(F=\mu R\), where \(F=|f|\).
A value beyond the limit is a sign that there is no equilibrium. Do not report the required balance force as actual friction when it is unavailable.

blocks.title: Compare required and available friction
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(65\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of \(10\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.

retry.feedback: Compare the required friction to the limit. They are equal, so this is specifically limiting equilibrium.

blocks.hint: Calculate the friction demanded by zero resultant first. Compare its magnitude, not its signed value, with the limit.
blocks.solution:
Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=60-\left(0\right)=60\).

With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=25-10=15\).

The required friction has magnitude \(15\,\mathrm N\) and would act uphill.

The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{4}\times 60=15\).

Required signed friction is \(15\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(15\,\mathrm N\). The particle is in limiting equilibrium. Friction is at its available limit.

sections.title: Must friction always point up an incline?
sections.label: Check which way slip is tending
sections.intro: Weight alone tends to pull a particle down the slope, but an applied force may exceed that effect. To find friction, compare the tangential force components before including friction.

blocks.html: With uphill positive, \(f=W\sin\alpha-P_{\parallel}\). Positive \(f\) acts uphill, negative \(f\) downhill, and \(f=0\) indicates no friction.

figure.alt: The external force P points uphill and the friction force F points downhill, with weight down and reaction perpendicular to the plane.
figure.caption: In this possible equilibrium, the applied force would otherwise make the particle slip uphill. That is why the friction arrow points downhill.

blocks.html: Friction does not automatically act uphill, and there may be no static friction despite rough contact.

blocks.title: Compare required and available friction
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(130\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of \(50\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.
blocks.hint: Calculate the friction demanded by zero resultant first. Compare its magnitude, not its signed value, with the limit.
blocks.solution:
Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=120-\left(0\right)=120\).

With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=50-50=0\).

The required friction has magnitude \(0\,\mathrm N\).

The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{4}\times 120=30\).

Required signed friction is \(0\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(30\,\mathrm N\). Equilibrium is possible and is below the limiting condition.

sections.title: How does an angled pull change the friction limit?
sections.label: Find the reaction first
sections.intro: An oblique pull can reduce the normal reaction by partly supporting the weight. A push into the surface can increase it. The friction limit changes with the reaction.

blocks.html: On a horizontal floor, an upward force component \(P_y\) gives \(R=W-P_y\). A signed negative \(P_y\) makes the reaction larger than \(W\).
The reaction does not automatically equal the weight. Resolve across the surface before multiplying by \(\mu\).

blocks.title: Resolve before using the friction limit
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(96\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough horizontal floor. A force of \(45\,\mathrm N\) acts below the horizontal to the right. The acute angle \(\beta\) satisfies \(\tan \beta=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the normal reaction, the friction magnitude required for equilibrium and the maximum friction. Decide whether the particle can be in equilibrium.
blocks.hint: An applied force can change the normal reaction. Balance vertically before finding the friction limit.
blocks.solution:
Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Resolve the applied force: \(36\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(-27\,\mathrm N\) upwards.

Vertical equilibrium gives \(R=123\). Then \(\mu R=41\).

The required friction is less than the maximum. The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

The normal reaction is \(123\,\mathrm N\), required friction is \(36\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(41\,\mathrm N\). The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

sections.title: What is the full contact force?
sections.label: Combine contact components
sections.intro: The phrase normal reaction refers only to the component perpendicular to the surface. The full contact force is the vector sum of the normal reaction and friction.

blocks.html: The two contact components are perpendicular, so total contact-force magnitude is \(\sqrt{R^2+f^2}\).
Use the friction found from equilibrium. Do not replace it with the maximum unless the particle is at the limit.

blocks.title: Combine the two contact components
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(65\,\mathrm N\) rests on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. An applied force of \(17\,\mathrm N\) acts uphill along the plane. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the exact magnitude of the total contact force.
blocks.hint: Use the actual friction from equilibrium. The two perpendicular components do not add as ordinary magnitudes.
blocks.solution:
The normal force and friction are perpendicular components of a single contact force.

Balance normal and uphill components. The reaction is \(60\,\mathrm N\) and the signed uphill friction is \(8\,\mathrm N\). Its magnitude is at most \(15\,\mathrm N\), so equilibrium is feasible.

By Pythagoras the magnitude of the total contact force is \(\sqrt{60^2+\left(8\right)^2}=4 \sqrt{229}\) newtons.

The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.

A force of \(60\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{2}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.
solution: Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=60-\left(0\right)=60\).
With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=45-60=-15\).
The required friction has magnitude \(15\,\mathrm N\) and would act downhill.
The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{2}\times 60=30\).
Required signed friction is \(-15\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(30\,\mathrm N\). Equilibrium is possible and is below the limiting condition.

examples.title: Resolve before using the friction limit

The acute angle \(\beta\) satisfies \(\tan \beta=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{2}{5}\). Find the normal reaction, the friction magnitude required for equilibrium and the maximum friction. Decide whether the particle can be in equilibrium.
solution: Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Resolve the applied force: \(16\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(12\,\mathrm N\) upwards.
Vertical equilibrium gives \(R=73\). Then \(\mu R=\frac{146}{5}\).
The required friction is less than the maximum. The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

examples.title: Combine the two contact components
examples.question: A particle of weight \(50\,\mathrm N\) rests on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. An applied force of \(15\,\mathrm N\) acts uphill along the plane. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the exact magnitude of the total contact force.
solution: The normal force and friction are perpendicular components of a single contact force.
Balance normal and uphill components. The reaction is \(40\,\mathrm N\) and the signed uphill friction is \(15\,\mathrm N\). Its magnitude is at most \(20\,\mathrm N\), so equilibrium is feasible.

sections.title: What is the least coefficient that permits rest?
sections.label: Find the minimum coefficient
sections.intro: First calculate how much friction the forces demand and how strongly the particle presses on the plane. Then find the coefficient for which the available friction first meets that demand.

blocks.html: If \(R>0\), then \(\mu\ge\frac{|f|}{R}\). The right side is the minimum. The same expression equals the coefficient if the body is stated to be about to slip.
Use the magnitude of friction. A negative signed friction gives direction, not a negative coefficient.

blocks.title: Find the minimum coefficient of friction
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(104\,\mathrm N\) is at rest on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. An applied force of \(16\,\mathrm N\) acts horizontally towards the higher side of the plane. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). Find the least possible coefficient of friction.
blocks.hint: Solve for the actual friction needed, then divide its magnitude by the normal reaction.
blocks.solution:
Resolve perpendicular to the plane to obtain \(R=\frac{1328}{13}\). The applied force contributes \(- \frac{80}{13}\,\mathrm N\) outwards.

Resolve along the plane to find the signed friction required. Using uphill as positive gives \(f=\frac{328}{13}\). The friction is uphill.

For equilibrium \(|f|\le\mu R\). The minimum occurs when equality first becomes possible.

The least coefficient is \(\mu_{\min}=\frac{\frac{328}{13}}{\frac{1328}{13}}=\frac{41}{166}\).

sections.title: What slope can an unassisted particle just hold?
sections.label: Find the limiting inclination
sections.intro: With just weight and the reaction from the rough plane, equilibrium needs friction uphill. Check the ratio of the downhill weight component to the normal weight component.

blocks.html: \(W\sin\alpha\le\mu W\cos\alpha\) leads to \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\) on \(0\le\alpha<90^\circ\).
The coefficient of friction is a ratio and has no units of angle. Use inverse tangent to find the angle in degrees.

blocks.title: Find the greatest angle for equilibrium
blocks.prompt: A particle rests on a rough plane with no applied force other than its weight and the contact force. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{3}{8}\). Find the greatest possible angle of the plane above the horizontal, to one decimal place.
blocks.hint: Divide the weight component down the plane by the normal reaction, and take the inverse tangent when friction is limiting.
blocks.solution:
At inclination \(\alpha\) the uphill friction required is \(W\sin\alpha\) and the normal reaction is \(W\cos\alpha\).

Demand cannot exceed capacity, so \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\). On the acute interval tangent increases with the angle.

The limiting angle is \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{8}\right)=20.6^\circ\).

sections.title: How can a force be both too small and too large?
sections.label: Find two bounds
sections.intro: With an uphill pull, too little can let the particle slip down, while too much can make it tend to slip up. Keep one fixed positive direction so the same inequality detects both cases.

blocks.html: For a parallel pull, \(-\mu W\cos\alpha\le W\sin\alpha-P\le\mu W\cos\alpha\). Intersect the result with \(P\ge0\).
Using only the downhill-slip boundary misses the upper limit. Both limiting end-values are allowed when static friction can reach the limit.

blocks.title: Find both bounds for a holding force
blocks.prompt: A particle of weight \(78\,\mathrm N\) is held in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of magnitude \(P\) newtons acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{6}\). Find the inclusive range of \(P\).
blocks.hint: Write a single signed expression for friction. Then use both sides of its limit inequality.
blocks.solution:
Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=72\). Uphill balance gives \(f=30 - P\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(P\ge 18\), so \(P\ge 18\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(P\le 42\), so \(P\le 42\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(18\le P\le 42\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.

sections.title: What if changing the pull changes the normal force as well?
sections.label: Keep the reaction variable
sections.intro: Resolve normal to the surface to express \(R\) in terms of \(P\). Keep this expression in both sides of \(|f|\le\mu R\), and check contact across the proposed interval.

blocks.html: Split into \(f\le\mu R\) and \(-f\le\mu R\). Solve each signed inequality, checking the sign of any coefficient you divide by.

figure.alt: A horizontal force P acts towards the rise of the plane. The weight goes down and reaction points out of the surface. The possible friction direction is omitted.
figure.caption: The horizontal pull both holds the particle up the slope and presses it into the slope. The friction direction depends on the pull magnitude.

blocks.html: Do not use one constant value of \(R\) across the range when the pull has a normal component.
At each true slipping boundary, substitute the force back into both component equations to check the direction of the limiting friction.

sections.title: Why might an algebraic lower bound be negative?

blocks.html: A magnitude satisfies \(P\ge0\). Contact requires \(R\ge0\); if \(R=0\), the available friction is also zero.
A negative answer for a magnitude is not a force pointing the other way unless the problem explicitly defines a signed force.

extraPractice.prompt: A particle of weight \(104\,\mathrm N\) is held in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of magnitude \(P\) newtons acts uphill at angle \(\beta\) above the line of greatest slope, measured in the vertical cross-section. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The acute angle \(\beta\) satisfies \(\tan \beta=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{3}{5}\). Find the inclusive range of \(P\).
extraPractice.hint: Write a single signed expression for friction. Then use both sides of its limit inequality.
extraPractice.solution:
Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=96 - \frac{3 P}{5}\). Uphill balance gives \(f=40 - \frac{4 P}{5}\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(\frac{11}{25}P\ge - \frac{88}{5}\), so \(P\ge -40\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(\frac{29}{25}P\le \frac{488}{5}\), so \(P\le \frac{2440}{29}\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(0\le P\le \frac{2440}{29}\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.
